title: DGSAM: Domain Generalization via Individual Sharpness-Aware Minimization
main_claims: Global SAM in domain generalization can converge to fake flat minima where the total loss surface is flat but individual domain losses remain sharp, undermining cross-domain robustness.
Individual sharpness (per-domain) provides a valid upper bound on average worst-case domain risk, while global sharpness does not.
DGSAM's gradual domain-wise perturbation achieves both fine-grained individual sharpness control and lower computational overhead than standard SAM.
methodology: The authors formalize the fake flat minima problem theoretically (Proposition 3.1, Theorem 3.2) and propose DGSAM, which performs S+1 sequential domain-specific gradient ascent steps followed by an aggregated descent update. They prove epsilon-stationarity convergence (Theorem 4.1). Experiments follow the DomainBed protocol on five benchmarks (PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, TerraIncognita, DomainNet) using ResNet-50 pretrained on ImageNet, comparing against 20 baselines including SAM, SAGM, GSAM, and SWAD.
key_results: DGSAM achieves the highest average accuracy 67.2% and lowest domain-level variance 10.3 across five DomainBed benchmarks, outperforming SAM (64.5%), SWAD (66.9%), and SAGM (66.1%).
DGSAM reduces individual sharpness more effectively than SAM: on DomainNet, SAM shows mean individual sharpness of 4.79 vs. DGSAM's lower values, while SAM fails to flatten individual domain losses.
DGSAM combined with SWAD reaches 67.8% average accuracy, suggesting complementary mechanisms.
Computational cost of DGSAM (0.169 s/iter) is lower than SAM (0.217 s/iter) and similar to ERM (0.110 s/iter).
limitations: Theoretical analysis assumes the fake flat minima phenomenon but does not prove it always occurs for standard SAM in practice.
DGSAM requires domain labels during training, limiting applicability to settings without domain annotations.
The convergence theorem assumes standard smoothness conditions that may not fully hold for deep networks.
relevance_to_rq: Supporting relevance: this paper shows that global SAM's flatness can be misleading in multi-domain settings because it may not reduce per-domain sharpness. This is relevant to the RQ's examination of whether SAM's flatness explanation is sufficient — specifically the sam_mechanism and flat_minima_for_dg sub-topics. However, it focuses on multi-source domain generalization rather than the CIFAR-C single-source corruption robustness setting in our study.
